teaser: The king's former mistress needed a new image. Her painter hid it in a statue.
review_notes:
CATALOG MISMATCH: the supplied image is Boucher's standing portrait of Madame de Pompadour in a garden, dated 1759, in the Wallace Collection, London. It is NOT the 1756 reclining portrait in the Alte Pinakothek, Munich, named in the metadata. The lesson describes the image supplied (1759, Wallace Collection). Either the image or the year/museum must be corrected.
Statue group identified by the Wallace Collection as Friendship consoling Love; related to Pigalle's sculptures for Pompadour (Madame de Pompadour as Friendship, 1753).
Dog identified as Inès, one of her two pet dogs.
Boucher's failing eyesight in his later years is traditional.
End of the physical relationship with Louis XV is usually dated around 1750-1751.
Canvas size about 91 x 68 cm.

lesson.text: In 1759 François Boucher was 56 and had more work than any painter in France. He ran the design side of the royal tapestry factory, supplied models for porcelain, painted scenery for the opera and still turned out canvases by the dozen. His eyes were beginning to tire. And one client came before all the others, as she had for more than ten years.

She was born Jeanne-Antoinette Poisson, a financier's daughter with no noble blood. In 1745 Louis XV made her his official mistress and gave her a title: Marquise de Pompadour. By 1759 the love affair had been over for years. Yet she still lived at Versailles, advised the king daily and helped choose his ministers. How do you paint that?

“Poisson” means “fish” in French. Her enemies at court never let her forget it. Mocking songs about her circulated in Paris under the name “poissonnades,” and getting caught writing one could mean prison.

Boucher had painted her many times. Three years earlier he had shown her reclining indoors in a green dress with a book, the woman of taste and learning. This time he takes her into a garden, stands her up, and puts the real message of the picture behind her right shoulder, in the shade.

lesson.title: The message in stone
lesson.text: The pale shape at upper left is a statue. Read it from top to bottom.

spots.title: A woman looks down
spots.text: A stone woman with curled hair bends her head gently. One hand rests on her chest. She stands for Friendship.

spots.title: A child reaches up
spots.text: A winged child stretches both arms toward her. This is Cupid, the god of love, and he is the one being comforted. Love is the small figure here, and Friendship the large one.

spots.title: Her arm on the base
spots.text: Pompadour leans her elbow on the statue's pedestal, pearls at her wrist. She claims the sculpture as her own emblem.

lesson.text: Friendship consoling Love: this was her official story. Passion had ended and something steadier had replaced it. She repeated the theme everywhere. A few years before, she had the sculptor Jean-Baptiste Pigalle carve her in marble as Friendship itself. Boucher's painted statue is a cousin of those garden marbles.
The statue is not the only loyal companion in the garden. A much smaller one sits lower down, half hidden among roses, and it is alive.
Pompadour brought a pet along. Where is it sitting?

spots.title: Inès
spots.text: A small black-and-white spaniel perched on a green garden bench, head turned up toward her mistress. Her name was Inès. In portraits a dog meant faithfulness.

lesson.text: Statue and spaniel say the same thing twice: constancy. Both look toward her, and she looks at us. Now consider everything else in the picture, because it argues for something different. It argues for pleasure. This is Rococo, the light, curving, pastel style of mid-18th-century France, and Boucher was its most successful painter.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Powdered gray hair, small pearls, and two round patches of rouge. At Versailles heavy pink on the cheeks was a sign of rank. She was 37 or 38.

spots.title: The collar
spots.text: A band of ruffled lace tied around the neck instead of a necklace. Boucher builds it from tiny curls of white and gray.

spots.title: A ladder of bows
spots.text: Ribbon bows run down the front of the bodice, each one smaller than the last. The row leads the eye down to the narrow waist.

spots.title: The rose
spots.text: One pink rose pinned at the neckline, the same color as her cheeks. More roses grow beside the bench and lie cut on the ground at her feet.

spots.title: The gown
spots.text: Peach-pink silk under bands of frothy lace and gauze. The skirt takes up nearly half the canvas, spread wide over hoops at the hips.

spots.title: The fan
spots.text: A closed fan dangles from her fingertips, pointing down, right above the dog. Her hand is completely relaxed.

spots.title: One shoe
spots.text: The tip of a pale silk slipper peeks out under the hem. It is the only sign that there are feet under all that fabric.

lesson.text: A court portrait is an argument. Here the dress speaks of beauty and wealth, and the statue and the dog speak of loyalty. Together they claim that Pompadour was the king's friend, and that her place at court was secure.

Pompadour made art herself. She learned to engrave, which means cutting a design into a metal plate to print it on paper, and published a set of prints. Boucher helped as her teacher and reworked some of the plates.

The canvas is modest in size, about 91 by 68 centimeters (36 by 27 inches), a picture for a private room. It is the last portrait Boucher painted of her. She died at Versailles in 1764, at 42, worn out by lung disease. The king is said to have watched her coffin leave in the rain.

Boucher lost his protector just as taste was turning. The critic Denis Diderot attacked his sweet colors and rosy flesh as false and frivolous, and younger artists wanted Roman virtue instead. He was still named First Painter to the King in 1765, and died in 1770 in his studio at the Louvre.

Her name outlived the criticism. The royal porcelain factory at Sèvres, which she championed, produced a famous pink glaze later known as “rose Pompadour.” And the hairstyle swept up high off the forehead still carries her title.

Today the portrait hangs in the Wallace Collection in London, a short walk from Fragonard's The Swing, which borrowed its Cupid from a statue she had ordered. Two paintings from the same world: in one a secret is being kept, in the other a reputation is being built.

quiz.question: What does the statue behind Madame de Pompadour represent?
quiz.explanation: A woman, Friendship, comforts the small winged Cupid.

quiz.question: Why was that theme useful to her in 1759?
options: Her love affair with the king was over, but she remained his friend and adviser
She was about to marry the king
She was leaving the court for a convent
quiz.explanation: She presented her position as a lasting friendship.

quiz.question: What does the little spaniel stand for in a portrait like this?
quiz.explanation: Dogs were a common sign of loyalty.

quiz.question: What was Boucher's situation when he painted this?
options: He was a young unknown looking for a first client
He was 56, overloaded with work, and had served her for over a decade
quiz.explanation: He was the busiest painter in France and she was his main client.

quiz.question: Which critic attacked Boucher's style as false and frivolous?
quiz.explanation: Diderot disliked his sweet colors and rosy flesh.

facts.text: Madame de Pompadour was born into one of the oldest noble families of France.
facts.explanation: She was born Jeanne-Antoinette Poisson, a financier's daughter with no noble blood.

facts.text: Pompadour learned to engrave and published her own prints.
facts.explanation: Boucher taught her and helped with some of the plates.

facts.text: In the statue, Cupid is the large figure and Friendship the small one.
facts.explanation: It is the reverse: Friendship is large and comforts a small Cupid.
